articles.title: Bipartisan US Lawmakers Push Back On Trump's Russia Policy, Vow Support For Ukraine - Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty
articles.summary: Bipartisan US Lawmakers Push Back On Trump's Russia Policy, Vow Support For Ukraine  Radio Free Europe/Radio LibertyTrump’s Overtures to Putin Put Republican Candidates in Hot Seat  WSJGOP’s Don Bacon rips Trump over ‘disgraceful’ behavior on Ukraine, Russia  The HillRubio says Trump to take up to 60 days to weigh Russia sanctions  ReutersRepublicans revolt over Trump’s sanctions waiver for Russia  The Times
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON -- A bipartisan group of US lawmakers is stepping up efforts to defend Ukraine, challenging President Donald Trump’s decision to ease restrictions on Russian energy imports and demanding guarantees that Kyiv will retain access to critical American military and intelligence support.
In a series of legislative initiatives, congressional inquiries, and appeals to the administration, Republicans and Democrats have warned that decisions benefiting Moscow or disrupting Ukraine’s battlefield capabilities could undermine US national security, weaken congressional authority, and prolong Russia’s war.
The pushback comes after the administration authorized transactions involving Russian diesel fuel, amid reports that Ukraine’s access to SpaceX’s Starlink and military-grade Starshield satellite communications systems had been restricted.
Ukrainian officials say the disruptions have affected military operations, although they reported on October 24 that satellite connection speeds had been restored. Questions remain about who imposed the restrictions.
A Ukrainian official familiar with the matter told RFE/RL that SpaceX had not responded to Kyiv about the previous restrictions. The official added that although Kyiv had been in touch with the US government, "no one has explained what happened or what will happen next."
The developments have exposed growing divisions over the administration’s Russia policy, with some Republicans joining Democrats in demanding accountability and stronger safeguards for Ukraine.
Bill Targets Russian Oil Waiver
Representative Brian Fitzpatrick, a Pennsylvania Republican and co-chair of the Congressional Ukraine Caucus, has introduced the Ronald Reagan Peace Through Strength Act of 2026, alongside Republican Representative Don Bacon of Nebraska and Democratic Representative Marie Gluesenkamp Perez of Washington.
The bill would nullify a Treasury Department waiver issued on October 9 that authorized transactions involving Russian diesel fuel, including imports into the United States. The temporary authorization is due to expire on April 7, 2027.
Trump has defended the agreement with Russia as a way to increase global diesel supplies and bring down fuel prices. Announcing the deal on October 9 following talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin, he said Russia had agreed to immediately supply more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel to US and global markets, with further shipments to follow. Diesel prices have risen sharply amid disruptions to global energy supplies linked to the war in Iran.
The proposed bill would also prohibit future waivers allowing Russian energy imports and require intelligence agencies to provide support for Ukraine’s defense, notifying congressional intelligence committees within 24 hours of any interruption.
The legislation seeks to reinforce a 2022 federal law prohibiting Russian oil imports, which the sponsors say the administration has undermined through its latest decision.
“Congress must be a check to the president’s egregious appeasement to Putin,” Bacon told RFE/RL.
In a statement announcing the bill, Fitzpatrick argued that Washington could not credibly demand accountability from Russian President Vladimir Putin while allowing American markets to support the energy revenues sustaining his war.
“We must not import a single drop of Russian oil,” Fitzpatrick said, adding that Congress had approved the prohibition with overwhelming bipartisan support in 2022.
He invoked the late President Reagan’s foreign policy doctrine, arguing that strength was necessary to secure peace and that aggression must carry a cost greater than its rewards.
Bacon accused Trump of reversing his own criticism of European countries for purchasing Russian energy.
“For years, President Trump criticized Europe for buying Russian energy and propping up Putin’s war economy,” Bacon said. “Now, Trump wants to make it easier for Putin to sell diesel fuel. He is wrong.”
Gluesenkamp Perez also condemned the waiver, saying it ran roughshod over American national interests and the bipartisan will of Congress. She argued that if Trump wanted to reduce gasoline prices, he should pursue policies that end the war in Iran rather than direct American money toward Russia.
The bill has been referred to three House committees for consideration. Its introduction marks one of the first legislative responses to the administration’s recent Russia-related decisions.
Lawmakers Press Pentagon Over Ukraine Satellite Access
Concern over Ukraine’s military capabilities has also brought together lawmakers from both parties in the House and Senate.
Eight lawmakers -- Representatives Marcy Kaptur (Dem.-Ohio), Brian Fitzpatrick (Rep.-Pennsylvania), Mike Quigley (Dem.-Illinois), Jim Costa (Dem.-California), and Jimmy Panetta (Dem.-California), along with Senators Mark Kelly (Dem.-Arizona), Thom Tillis (Rep.-North Carolina), and Elissa Slotkin (Dem.-Michigan) -- have urged Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to expand the Pentagon’s Starshield contract and ensure uninterrupted access to Starlink and Starshield services.
The lawmakers called for the restoration of unrestricted service speeds, sufficient geographic coverage for Ukraine’s lawful military operations, including over Russian territory, and a seamless transition from commercial Starlink to government-contracted Starshield.
“Any degradation in service, including reduced connection speeds, restricted geographic coverage, or interruptions in access, undermines Ukraine’s military effectiveness and provides Russian forces with an operational advantage that will extend the conflict and put more civilians in harm’s way,” they wrote.
They also urged the Defense Department to consider using its authority under the Defense Production Act to ensure reliable access to the satellite communications on which Ukrainian forces depend for command and control, intelligence sharing, battlefield communications and drone operations.
“Decisions regarding service availability, coverage, and performance should not be left solely to the discretion of a private provider when they have direct consequences for Ukraine’s ability to defend itself,” the lawmakers said.
The appeal followed Ukrainian reports that restrictions introduced on October 13 disrupted communications for drones and other military platforms moving faster than 100 miles per hour (160 km/h), affecting Ukraine’s ability to guide defensive drones and conduct operations against Russian positions.
Musk Faces Questions Over Ukraine Satellite Restrictions
The satellite dispute has prompted additional congressional investigations into who ordered the restrictions and whether the US government has sufficient oversight of the communications systems it relies on.
New York Representative Gregory Meeks, the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, and Democratic Senator Peter Welch of Vermont have led a group of six Democratic lawmakers demanding answers from SpaceX chief executive Elon Musk.
Their letter questions Musk’s public assertion that restrictions were determined by the US military and ultimately the president, citing reports that Musk himself proposed limiting Ukrainian communications.
The lawmakers have asked whether Musk or SpaceX officials discussed restricting access with Trump, Putin, or their representatives; who ordered any limitations; what conditions Ukraine must meet to regain full access; and who will control future operational decisions.
They also raised concerns about corporate governance and the implications of a private company exercising decisive influence over a foreign military’s communications.
Connecticut Senator Richard Blumenthal, the top Democrat on the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, has separately opened a congressional inquiry, demanding written answers from Musk by November 5 and a briefing from SpaceX officials by November 12.
Blumenthal is seeking details about who authorized the restrictions, whether Ukraine received advance notice, and whether SpaceX can degrade Starshield service for US or allied forces without Pentagon authorization. He has also requested information on the value of SpaceX’s government contracts since 2020.
Separately, Democratic Representatives Sam Liccardo and Ro Khanna of California, along with Panetta, have called on White House chief of staff Susie Wiles to initiate a government-wide investigation and provide a briefing within two weeks.
“Either a private contractor independently made life-and-death national security decisions, or President Trump directed the restriction of critical military communications supporting a US ally,” they wrote.
The demands for answers come amid conflicting accounts of who authorized the restrictions.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio has denied that Trump or other administration officials ordered them or knew about them in advance. Musk, meanwhile, has said Starshield systems are controlled by the US government and that decisions on restrictions ultimately rest with the military and the president.
Trump has said service was restored following contact with Musk, but Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has disputed that account, saying restrictions remain in place.
The uncertainty has also drawn criticism from Republican Senator Thom Tillis, who wrote on X: “Whoever is handing Putin the gift of a more vulnerable Ukraine should at least have the guts to put their name on it.”

articles.title: Piyush Goyal Slams Europes Climate Policies Over Carbon Emissions, Warns CBAM And Steel Import Tariffs Could - Free Press Journal
articles.summary: Piyush Goyal Slams Europes Climate Policies Over Carbon Emissions, Warns CBAM And Steel Import Tariffs Could  Free Press Journal
articles.full_text:
New Delhi: Union Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal strongly criticised Europe's climate policies on Friday, arguing that developed nations bear greater historical responsibility for global carbon emissions and climate change.
Speaking at the Berlin Global Dialogue 2026, Goyal warned that Europe's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) and high steel import duties could increase living costs and weaken industrial competitiveness.
Piyush Goyal Questions Europe's Climate Responsibility
During a panel discussion, Goyal questioned developed countries' historical contribution to the climate crisis. He argued that India supports approximately 17 per cent of the global population but contributes less than 3 per cent of carbon emissions.
In contrast, he said Europe's contribution to global emissions has been disproportionately high compared with its population. Goyal maintained that developed economies relied heavily on inexpensive fossil fuels during their industrial expansion.
CBAM And Steel Tariffs Could Raise Costs
The minister criticised Europe's carbon border tax and steel import restrictions, warning that such measures could affect businesses and consumers. He argued that imposing additional costs on imported products could make European industries less competitive while increasing household expenses. Goyal also highlighted India's growing renewable energy programme and commitment to sustainable development.
India Raises Climate Finance Concerns
Referring to the 2015 Paris Agreement, Goyal emphasised the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities. Under this framework, developed nations are expected to take greater responsibility for addressing climate change and supporting developing economies. He questioned the delivery of the promised USD 100 billion annual climate financing commitment, alleging that financial support remained inadequate.
Piyush Goyal's Germany Visit
Goyal is visiting Germany and the Netherlands from October 22 to 27, accompanied by approximately 100 Indian businesses and startups. His remarks highlight continuing differences between India and Europe over carbon emissions, climate financing and trade-related environmental regulations.

articles.title: Could France's bond turmoil force the ECB's hand? - Euronews.com
articles.summary: Could France's bond turmoil force the ECB's hand?  Euronews.com
articles.full_text:
The European Central Bank is expected to hold rates next week as France's bond sell-off tightens borrowing conditions across the eurozone, while ECB President Christine Lagarde has made clear that the first steps to tackle French debt woes must come from Paris, not Frankfurt.
When the European Central Bank (ECB) meets next Thursday, it is widely expected to leave interest rates unchanged, partly because rising government bond yields are already pushing up borrowing costs across the eurozone.
ECB President Christine Lagarde has played down hopes of a rescue, saying the solution to France's debt problems lies at home.
The yield on France's 10-year government bond traded above 5% on Friday after rising to that level on Wednesday for the first time since 2002. The gap with German 10-year bonds, the eurozone's safest debt, was above 170 basis points.
Meanwhile, the 30-year yield was at 5.5%, and the gap with German 30-year bonds was even wider at 184 basis points.
On Thursday, the cost of France's five-year credit default swaps, contracts that insure investors against a government default, also climbed above 100 basis points for the first time since October 2012, when the eurozone was going through its sovereign debt crisis.
Lawmakers remain split over next year's budget, which includes €43 billion in spending cuts and additional revenue measures that the government has no majority to push through.
Despite the recent market movements, ratings agency Moody's maintained its Aa3 credit rating for France on Friday evening, albeit with a negative outlook. S&P and Fitch have their ratings one-notch lower.
Civil unrest is adding to investors' concerns.
More protests are expected this weekend, and Paris police prefect Patrice Faure has advised business owners in a letter to hire private security.
French trade unions, unanimously disappointed after meeting Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu on Wednesday, have called for a large mobilisation on 5 November.
Sophie Binet, head of the CGT, one of France's biggest unions, urged workers to "generalise the strike".
Bonds doing the ECB's job
The case for another rate hike is still there.
The ECB has raised rates twice this year, lifting its deposit rate to 2.5%, and eurozone inflation jumped to 3.8% in September, driven by energy prices.
Yet German yields have climbed so much since September that their effect on growth and inflation roughly matches a 25 basis point hike, Carsten Brzeski, global head of macro at Dutch bank ING, estimated in an investor note on Thursday.
"For France, it’s closer to a 50 basis point hike," Brzeski wrote, adding that "the bond market has taken over the ECB's job".
Brzeski expects the ECB to wait for new staff forecasts in December before deciding on its next hike.
ECB President Christine Lagarde told the European Parliament on 28 September that long-term rates "have risen notably, which will slow growth".
Could the ECB intervene?
ECB officials have played down the possibility of intervening to lower France's borrowing costs, but have stopped short of ruling it out.
The central bank bought government bonds during the eurozone debt crisis to stabilise markets and ensure its rate decisions continued to feed through to the economy.
Speaking on the sidelines of the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank in Bangkok last week, Lagarde said that "there are particular circumstances that lead to some countries being more affected, France being a case in point."
"The primary and first solution lies at home in France. And it has to do with fiscal policies," the ECB president added.
Banque de France governor Emmanuel Moulin went further last Friday, saying the conditions for ECB intervention were not met at that time because there was no financial fragmentation in the eurozone.
However, both officials spoke before France’s 10-year borrowing costs rose above 5%.
If the ECB decides to intervene in the French bond market, one option could be the Transmission Protection Instrument (TPI), which was created in 2022 and has never been used.
The TPI lets the ECB buy the debt of countries whose borrowing costs climb in ways it judges unjustified by their economic fundamentals and threaten the transmission of monetary policy across the eurozone.
For a country to be eligible, it needs to meet several criteria, including following EU fiscal rules and keeping its debt on a sustainable path.
France is nursing a debt-to-GDP ratio of 119.1%, and the current budget negotiations offer little prospect of a quick reduction in the deficit, which is necessary to put the debt on a sustainable path.
Meanwhile, the government expects its debt-servicing costs to rise by more than €10 billion in 2027 compared with this year.
"The bar for activating the ECB's bond-buying programme remains high," Brzeski wrote in a separate investor note last week.
He added that, for France, that would at least mean passing its full budget. Acting too early could be "interpreted as monetary financing of the debt of a country unwilling to follow the rules," he warned.
The ECB's other emergency tool, Outright Monetary Transactions (OMT), was created in 2012 at the height of the eurozone debt crisis to allow unlimited purchases of a struggling country's short-term bonds.
However, it is only available to governments that first sign up to a bailout programme from the eurozone's rescue fund, the European Stability Mechanism.
Instead, Brzeski expects the ECB to quietly pause the reduction of its bond holdings, reinvesting maturing debt flexibly as it did during the COVID-19 pandemic.
Should turmoil spread to other eurozone bond markets, Brzeski sees TPI as a last resort. If France continued to fall short of EU fiscal rules, "the ECB might even consider purchasing bonds from almost all eurozone countries, except for France," he said.
For now, Brzeski sees next week’s rate meeting as "uneventful on action but clearly not on words".

articles.title: EU AI Act - PPC Land
articles.summary: EU AI Act  PPC Land
articles.full_text:
The EU AI Act is the European Union's law on artificial intelligence (AI), formally Regulation (EU) 2024/1689. It sorts AI by the harm it can do rather than by the technology behind it: a short list of practices is banned outright, uses that affect jobs, credit, education or policing carry heavy compliance duties, systems that talk to people or generate content must disclose it, and everything else is left largely alone. A separate chapter covers the general-purpose models that power chatbots and image generators. The law exists because the EU decided product safety and fundamental rights rules written before machine learning could not reach decisions made by statistical systems at scale. It reaches companies anywhere whose AI is placed on the EU market or whose output is used there.
How the risk tiers work
The Act runs to 113 articles and 13 annexes. Article 3 defines an AI system as a machine-based system that "infers, from the input it receives, how to generate outputs such as predictions, content, recommendations, or decisions", the word "infers" separating it from rule-based software.
Prohibited practices under Article 5 sit at the top. Eight categories were banned from February 2, 2025, among them subliminal or manipulative techniques that materially distort behaviour, exploitation of vulnerabilities linked to age or disability, social scoring, untargeted scraping of facial images, emotion recognition in workplaces and schools, and most real-time remote biometric identification by police in public spaces. For advertisers the manipulation ban is the live question. Commission guidelines published in February 2025 separate permissible persuasion from prohibited manipulation, and ordinary persuasive advertising is not in scope unless it causes or is likely to cause significant harm.
High-risk systems form the second tier, and there are two routes in. Under Article 6(1), AI that is a safety component of a product already regulated by EU law listed in Annex I, such as machinery, medical devices or toys, is high-risk. Under Article 6(2), AI used in the eight areas of Annex III is high-risk: biometrics, critical infrastructure, education, employment, access to essential services including credit scoring and insurance pricing, law enforcement, migration, and justice and democratic processes. Article 6(3) offers an exit for Annex III systems that only perform a narrow procedural task or prepare a human decision, but never for systems that profile people.
A high-risk provider must run a risk management system, govern its training data, keep technical documentation and automatic logs, design for human oversight, meet accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity requirements, operate a quality management system under Article 17, pass a conformity assessment, affix a CE mark and register the system in an EU database. Deployers must assign trained human overseers, keep logs and, in the case of public bodies, banks and insurers, carry out a fundamental rights impact assessment under Article 27.
Transparency duties under Article 50 form the third tier. Chatbots must tell people they are talking to a machine. Providers of generative systems must mark output in a machine-readable way. Deployers must label deepfakes and AI-generated text published to inform the public.
General-purpose AI models sit beside the tiers rather than inside them. Since August 2, 2025, every provider owes technical documentation, a copyright policy and a public summary of training content under Article 53. Models trained with more than 10^25 floating-point operations are presumed to carry systemic risk and face evaluation, incident reporting and cybersecurity duties under Article 55. Supervision of these providers belongs to the Commission's AI Office; nearly everything else is enforced by national market surveillance authorities.
Fines under Article 99 are tiered: up to 35 million euros or 7% of worldwide annual turnover for prohibited practices, 15 million euros or 3% for most other breaches, and 7.5 million euros or 1% for supplying incorrect information. For small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), the lower of the two figures applies.
From white paper to law
The Commission published a white paper on AI in February 2020 and proposed the Act on April 21, 2021. That draft predated ChatGPT, and the European Parliament added rules for foundation models in June 2023. Trilogue talks ended on December 8, 2023 after nearly 15 hours of negotiation, according to RTE. "Historic! The EU becomes the very first continent to set clear rules for the use of AI," Thierry Breton, then internal market commissioner, wrote on X.
Parliament approved the text on March 13, 2024 by 523 votes to 46, with 49 abstentions, and the Council adopted it on May 21, 2024. Published in the Official Journal on July 12, 2024, the Act entered into force on August 1, 2024, with application staggered over three years.
The staggering soon came under strain. On July 3, 2025, more than 45 companies including ASML, Airbus and Mistral AI asked Commission President Ursula von der Leyen for a two-year postponement, according to The Decoder. "There is no grace period. There is no pause," Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier replied the next day. On September 16, 2025, Mario Draghi, former president of the European Central Bank, called for the high-risk stage to be "paused until we better understand the drawbacks".
The omnibus rewrite
The Commission's Digital Omnibus on AI, proposed on November 19, 2025, tied the high-risk dates to the availability of standards. Parliament's committees instead backed fixed deadlines in March 2026. Talks collapsed overnight in late April before a provisional agreement on May 7, 2026. The result, Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, was published on July 24 and entered into force on July 27, 2026.
As of October 2026, the timetable reads as follows. The general date of application, August 2, 2026, did not move, and Article 50 transparency duties apply from it. Annex III high-risk obligations move from August 2, 2026 to December 2, 2027. Annex I high-risk obligations move from August 2, 2027 to August 2, 2028. Generative systems already on the market before August 2, 2026 have until December 2, 2026 to meet the marking duty, the date on which new bans on AI tools generating non-consensual intimate imagery and child sexual abuse material also apply. The omnibus also extended SME relief to "small mid-caps" and handed the AI Office exclusive supervision of AI systems built on a provider's own model or embedded in very large online platforms, with periodic penalties of up to 5% of average daily turnover.
The AI literacy duty in Article 4, applicable since February 2, 2025, illustrates how sources still diverge. PPC Land's report on the May deal described the obligation moving from companies to the Commission and member states, which would "encourage and facilitate". Law firm Akin Gump, reading the published regulation, says providers and deployers must still take measures to "support the development of AI literacy", a softer obligation than the original but not a transfer.
Why it matters for marketers
Most advertising AI, from bid optimisation to copy generation, falls outside the high-risk annex. Three routes bring the Act closer.
The first is labelling. Since August 2, 2026, an advertiser or agency that publishes an AI-generated deepfake, such as a synthetic spokesperson, must disclose it, and Commission guidelines of July 2026 deny commercial advertising the lighter regime for artistic works. Fines reach 15 million euros or 3% of turnover.
The second is the supply chain. Ad platforms are providers and advertisers deployers. Since July 2026 the ranking, creative and bidding systems inside platforms such as Facebook, Instagram, YouTube and Google Search answer to the AI Office rather than national regulators. The third is the boundary: credit scoring, candidate filtering and personalisation that exploits vulnerabilities touch high-risk or prohibited territory.
Criticism and disputes
Enforcement architecture draws the most complaints. Member states had to designate national authorities by August 2, 2025, yet Cullen International counted only three national AI laws in force, in Denmark, Finland and Italy, as of April 2026. An initial Commission list contained around 2,000 notified market surveillance authorities, according to CMS. Germany's digital association, the Bundesverband Digitale Wirtschaft (BVDW), warned in October 2025 of jurisdictional conflicts between agencies.
Standards lag the law. Harmonised standards give providers a presumption of conformity, but the first, EN 18286 on quality management, was referenced in the Official Journal only on October 14, 2026, according to ActuIA. Nine of the ten areas in the Commission's standardisation request still had no harmonised standard. Draft guidelines on high-risk classification, initially expected by February 2, 2026, appeared on May 19, 2026, according to Hunton Andrews Kurth.
Scope is contested from both sides: industry calls the definitions vague, while creative-sector organisations rejected the implementation measures on training data as insufficient.
Not the same as
GDPR. The General Data Protection Regulation governs personal data processing; the AI Act governs the system as a product. Both can apply to one tool.
Digital Services Act (DSA). Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 sets content moderation and advertising transparency duties for platforms. The AI Act borrows its platform designations.
Council of Europe Framework Convention on AI. A treaty opened for signature on September 5, 2024 that binds states, not companies, and reaches beyond the EU.
Digital Omnibus. The 2025 amending package; its data part, covering the GDPR and cookies, is still under negotiation.

articles.title: How EU ships are still able to carry Trump's Russian diesel despite so many sanctions - The Kyiv Independent
articles.summary: How EU ships are still able to carry Trump's Russian diesel despite so many sanctions  The Kyiv IndependentUkraine war briefing: Russian diesel tankers headed for North America, says Moscow, as US tries to revive peace talks  The GuardianFirst Russian diesel tanker heads to New York after Trump's deal with Putin to lower fuel prices  Fox BusinessEXCLUSIVE: First Russian diesel from Putin-Trump deal heading for US, data shows  Reuters3 Tankers of Russian Di...
articles.full_text:
BRUSSELS, Belgium — When news broke on Oct. 23 that a ship was reportedly carrying a new supply of Russian diesel for U.S. President Donald Trump, one question immediately arose: How, after more than 20 rounds of EU sanctions, could European ships still be involved in facilitating that trade?
Trump's Oct. 9 deal to buy Russian diesel was part of a wider pivot towards Moscow that was met with widespread condemnation by EU leaders. The deal itself might also be illegal under U.S. sanctions policy.
However, media reports circulated on Oct. 23 that a ship called the Agioi Fanendes, which had just left Russia's Baltic Sea port of Primorsk, was carrying 40,000 metric tons to New York, and the ship has been traveling through the Baltic Sea westwards ever since.
Adding to the sense of mystery, ship-tracking website MarineTraffic noted that the Agioi Fanendes updated its status on Oct. 23 from heading to New York to, "for orders" — ship-speak for final destination unconfirmed.
That ship is owned by the Greek company Eastern Mediterranean Maritime, owned by billionaire Thanasis Martinos. It is flying under a Maltese flag. Both countries are part of the EU, so the Agioi Fanendes has to comply with the bloc's 21 sanctions packages imposed on Russia since it launched its full-scale invasion in 2022.
"EU law hasn't changed," wrote Ukraine's sanctions chief Vladyslav Vlasiuk on social media.
"An EU-flagged, EU-managed ship may carry Russian diesel only if it was bought at or below the $100 a barrel price cap," Vlasiuk said.
That price refers to the G7 oil price cap, agreed in 2022 to reduce the profits Russia can make from the oil trade while still ensuring the world's energy supply.
A European Commission spokesperson confirmed to the Kyiv Independent Vlasiuk's interpretation of what is legally possible.
"EU operators are only allowed to provide maritime transport and related services for Russian crude oil and petroleum products if these are sold at or below the relevant price caps," they said.
And written guidance prepared by the Commission makes explicit that shipowners also bear some responsibility for ensuring their cargo is compliant with sanctions.
"Shipowners should obtain from their customer an attestation in which the customer confirms the Russian oil cargo transported or to be transported has been purchased at or below the price cap."
When asked to confirm the financial value of Agioi Fanendes' cargo, a spokesperson for Eastern Mediterranean Maritime instead said "kindly be advised that Agioi Fanendes is proceeding for orders as discharging port is not confirmed yet."
They had not yet replied to a follow-up question confirming receipt of the EU-required attestation by the time of publication.
To get to the U.S., the Agioi Fanendes will first have to travel through the Baltic Sea, and if it enters the territorial waters of any EU country on the way — 12 miles from their shoreline, they can also intervene to stop the ship.
The Finnish Border Guard told the Kyiv Independent when the ship was just leaving that country's territorial waters that there was no planned intercept, and no information they could share.
Sweden's coastguard, which has previously boarded several Russian shadow fleet ships, said "we are monitoring the sea traffic in the Baltic Sea 24/7 and keep an updated and thorough situational awareness."
However, they declined to comment on specific ships, adding only that they "keep track of all oil transporting ships."
In the meantime, the Agioi Fanendes has moved via international waters in the center of the Baltic Sea. But in international water, the law of the country whose flag your ship is flying is the one that applies.
"Malta is firmly committed to the rigorous implementation of European Union sanctions and expects full compliance with all applicable restrictive measures," the country's sanctions unit told the Kyiv Independent.
"Vessels flying the Maltese flag are likewise required to comply fully with the sanctions applicable to them," they said.
"We are aware of the reports concerning this particular shipment, and the relevant attestations are being sought from the vessel's owners and operators," the Maltese sanctions unit confirmed.
Only when that attestation is provided that the diesel aboard the Agioi Fanendes complies with the G7 price cap can it legally satisfy the U.S.' thirst for Russian fossil fuels.
With the buyer, seller, and the agreed price of the diesel all unknown, according to the original Reuters article on the Agioi Fanendes, the only possible way to prove that the ship is not in breach of EU sanctions would be for that attestation Malta is waiting for to be provided.

SpaceX’s Starlink and Starshield satellite communications services have been restored in Ukraine, allowing the country's forces to operate drones at high speed, Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara said on Saturday.
"The Ministry of Defense's monitoring systems indicate that Starlink/Starshield speeds have been restored," Khmara told reporters in WhatsApp messages. "We are recording speeds exceeding 400 km/h, and the connection is stable."
Since last week, Kyiv had been reporting speed limits on Starshield, Starlink's military-grade service, affecting Ukraine's ability to use drones and carry out defensive strikes. The throttling came amid growing tensions between Washington and Kyiv, with Trump blaming President Volodymyr Zelenskyy for the continuation of the war with Russia.

SpaceX’s effort to turn Starlink Mobile into the US’s fourth major carrier might involve it buying access to tens of thousands of cell towers nationwide.
Bloomberg reports that SpaceX wants to secure “a minimum of 80,000 cell sites across the US,” and is already in talks with one major cellular infrastructure provider.
Earlier this week, cell tower operator Crown Castle also said it estimates SpaceX could provide an “additional catalyst” for its business, which covers 40,000 towers. Crown points to potential leasing agreements with SpaceX, as well as a competitive threat from Starlink Mobile that could prompt other carriers to bolster their own networks.
“I don’t want to get into customer details, but you can assume that we’re talking to all parties,” Crown Castle CEO Chris Hillabrant said in the earnings call when asked about SpaceX and other satellite companies.
Bloomberg’s report specifically uses “cell sites” rather than “cell towers.” Still, the 80,000 number is significant because AT&T, T-Mobile, and Verizon are estimated to have rented access to around the same number of cell towers across the US. A March report prepared for the Wireless Infrastructure Association estimates T-Mobile has the most at 82,000, while AT&T is at 75,000, and Verizon is at 65,000.
Still, it’s important to note that each carrier also operates “small cell sites” alongside its towers. The wireless trade group CTIA estimates that the US has 442,000 cell sites, with lower-powered small cell sites accounting for 40%.
These small cell sites can be built by placing backpack-sized radio transmitters on street lights, building sides, or poles. Each of the big three carriers has been estimated to operate between 45,000 and 90,000 outdoor small sites, according to Steel In The Air, which tracks cell lease negotiations.
For Starlink Mobile, SpaceX plans to use a combination of next-generation satellites, cell towers, and its own cost-effective radio transmitters, called femtocells, which could also be installed in people’s homes or businesses. In SpaceX’s earnings call this week, the company suggested it could sell the femtocell equipment to existing Starlink subscribers to help bolster coverage for Starlink Mobile in the US.
Still, industry analysts have been skeptical about SpaceX’s cellular ambitions, partly because it’ll likely cost the company tens of billions of dollars to build out the network. The company will also need to invest heavily in securing additional radio spectrum and building out its retail and customer support infrastructure.
Ken Schmidt, CEO of Steel In The Air, speculated that some of SpaceX’s recent moves might be about pressuring the big three carriers, which have seen their stock values drop on the Starlink Mobile competitive threat.
“I hope Starlink is serious about 80,000 sites; it's good for consumers, good for the tower industry, bad for the carriers, and good for landowners/building owners. But it seems like exactly what I would do if I wanted to pressure the Big 3 and force one to sign an MVNO deal, too,” Schmidt wrote on LinkedIn.
In other words, SpaceX could be using the cell site news as leverage to compel one of the big three carriers to enter a resale partnership with the Elon Musk-led company, giving it access to their terrestrial cell networks. But so far, executives for AT&T, T-Mobile, and Verizon have shot down the MVNO idea. T-Mobile is even a SpaceX partner, and the exclusive provider of the first-gen Starlink Mobile service in the US. But in recent months, the carrier has been downplaying the satellite connectivity, and even signaling it could use a different satellite provider.

articles.full_text:
Ukraine said it recaptured more of its territory than Russia had managed to seize this year, despite restrictions on US satellite services critical to its defence.
Russia responded by hitting dozens of Ukraine’s energy facilities and using cluster bombs in attacks that harmed civilians.
“Our soldiers have liberated more territory since the beginning of autumn than the Russians have managed to capture,” said Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in a public address.
Ukrainian General Staff spokesman Andriy Kovalev denied Russian claims to have seized 1,800 sq km (700 square miles) of Ukrainian territory during the autumn.
The Institute for the Study of War, a Washington-based think tank that uses geolocated open-source information to assess territorial movements, said Ukraine had made a net gain of 241 sq km (93 square miles) since September 1, effectively eliminating any Russian territorial gains this year.
Russia’s casualties suggest the effectiveness of its forces is in decline.
Russian losses – meaning those killed or severely wounded – hovered around 30,000 a month from January to May, but steadily increased over the summer. According to Ukrainian estimates, Russia lost 46,230 soldiers in September, its highest monthly losses of the year, and 37,000 so far in October.
October 21 marked its highest daily losses of the entire war, at 2,250, said Robert Brovdi, the commander of the Unmanned Systems Forces of Ukraine, as his unit’s kill rate had climbed to a new record.
Overall, Ukraine estimated there were more than 350,000 Russian dead and wounded since the beginning of the year.
Many of Ukraine’s territorial gains were made by Operation Vivaldi, a Ukrainian counteroffensive that stopped a Russian pincer movement to recapture the remaining one-fifth of Ukraine’s eastern Donetsk region – roughly 5,500 sq km (2,000 square miles).
General Andriy Biletskyi, who led Ukraine’s Third Army Corps to victory in that campaign, said he had eliminated a Russian bridgehead on the western bank of the Zherebets river, and crossed over to the east bank, shortening his own front line and concentrating artillery and unmanned aerial firepower, stabilising its defence.
The defeat of the pincer, said Biletskyi, had left Russia with the unsavoury option of a frontal assault on the “fortress belt” of heavily defended cities of Kramatorsk, Sloviansk and Druzhivka.
Russia had “temporarily abandoned this plan, although it plans to resume it,” Biletskyi told the Ukrainian news outlet Suspilne. Russian military expert Andrey Marochko told Russia’s state news agency TASS that Ukraine was reinforcing the fortress cities.
Russia has responded to its sagging military fortunes by increasing the ferocity of its attacks on civilians.
On October 22, it flew three ballistic missiles with cluster warheads into Kyiv, Zelenskyy said.
“This warhead detonates above the ground and is specifically designed to inflict maximum damage on people and equipment within an area of 400 by 400 metres,” said Ukrainian Defence Ministry senior adviser Serhiy Beskrestnov. “45 submunitions explode in the air.”
One of the warheads struck an area between the Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra cathedral and a monastery.
“There was not even theoretically any military object nearby,” said Zelenskyy. “It is a deliberate choice of weapons, a deliberate choice of the area.”
Russia’s Defence Ministry claimed it had targeted an assembly building for the FP-5 long-range drones and FP-9 missiles Ukraine has been using against it, as well as other drone manufacturing sites.
More than anything else, though, Russia has relentlessly targeted Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, despite United States President Donald Trump declaring an energy ceasefire for both sides on October 11.
Since then, there had been more than 170 strikes on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, Zelenskyy said.
“Russia is not achieving any significant results on the front lines. Therefore, it is directing all its aggression and hatred towards terrorising civilian infrastructure: electricity, heating, and now, water. The goal is clear – to exhaust the people,” Prime Minister Serhiy Khoretskyi told the BBC.
Since he assumed office on July 16, he said, Russia had attacked Ukraine’s energy infrastructure 2,147 times.
Ukraine has been hampered in its defence by the US, which on October 8 was understood to have stopped providing early warning of incoming ballistic missiles for the second time this year.
Zelenskyy said that early warning had been restored on October 20, but three other US actions detrimental to Ukraine’s defence had not been reversed.
One was Trump’s waiver of oil export sanctions on Russia to lower the price of diesel, which he formalised with an executive order on October 16. Putin said on October 21 that Russia’s first shipment of 40,000 tonnes of diesel to the US would depart within two or three days.
Another issue was that the US has not released Patriot interceptors to Ukraine, which are its most effective defence against ballistic missiles, despite having previously supplied a dozen a month, and despite the fact that Europe has paid for them.
But the biggest problem was that Ukraine’s ability to fly its drones at more than 150kmh (100mph) using the Starshield satellite navigation system remained suspended.
Ukraine has said it cannot intercept fast-moving jet-powered drones at such speeds, and its attacks on Russian logistics, as well as the resupply of its own front lines by drone, are also rendered more vulnerable.
Starshield was created as a military application of Starlink, owned by Elon Musk, and he and the White House traded blame for making the decision to restrict it throughout the week. Trump said on October 22 that Starlink and Starshield services were about to be restored.
After initially observing Trump’s energy ceasefire, Ukraine resumed targeting Russian energy infrastructure, as part of an economic strategy to starve the Russian war machine of export revenue.
On October 18, it struck the St Petersburg oil terminal, Russia’s biggest offloading terminal for oil exports. It also hit a data centre serving Russian social media platform Vkontakte, disrupting services.
Other facilities were likely targeted. Russia’s Defence Ministry said it had downed 1,015 Ukrainian drones over various regions that night.
The US appeared to leverage its waiver of diesel sanctions and the suspension of Starshield services to push for a trilateral meeting among the US, Russia and Ukraine.
US envoy Steve Witkoff met with Zelenskyy in Oslo on October 20, and followed up with a meeting with Putin in St Petersburg the following day.
Putin aide Yuri Ushakov told the media that Russia had agreed “in principle” to meet on November 10. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said the planned meeting would be held in Abu Dhabi.
